The coordinated transit of intestinal contents is crucial for digestion and host defense, and is regulated by cross-talk between neural circuits, the muscular gut wall and luminal factors. Here we show that androgen signaling to Nos1+ enteric neurons and Scn10a+ spinal afferent neurons is required for normal intestinal transit in mice and is microbiome dependent. Microbial depletion with antibiotics abolished androgen receptor expression in enteric neurons, diminished serum testosterone and caused dysmotility. Androgens were necessary for antibiotics to affect transit and partly sufficient to rescue dysmotility. Nos1 neurons upregulate androgen receptor upon puberty in parallel with shifts in fecal bacterial beta-glucuronidase (GUS) enzymes that can deconjugate steroid glucuronides in mice and humans. Intracolonic administration of a GUS enzyme found to metabolize androgen glucuronides was sufficient to restore neuronal androgen signaling in microbe-depleted mice. Thus, gut microbial reactivation of host-excreted androgens via GUS enzymes represents a dynamic microbe–host interaction that is essential for peripheral nervous system function in homeostasis.

The directed movement of gastrointestinal (GI) contents from ingestion to expulsion is essential for life. Gut motor activity is directed by the enteric nervous system (ENS), the complex neuroglial networks that constitute the intrinsic nervous system of the digestive tract. Gut bacteria can influence GI motility by generating factors that signal to the ENS, such as aryl hydrocarbon receptor ligands and bile acid metabolites1–5. Germ-free mice raised in gnotobiotic conditions1,2,4 or conventionally raised mice exposed to broad-spectrum antibiotics (ABX) both have

slowed intestinal transit6,7. None of the microbe-derived factors found to date, however, fully rescue the deficits in these mice, suggesting that additional factors remain to be found. We recently reported that gonadal androgens signal to neurons in the ENS to selectively regulate propulsive motor behaviors in the colon8. Cre recombinase lines were validated for each cell type to identify lines with Cre activity that was selective, without evidence of recombination in the epithelium (Extended Data Fig. 2a–g). ORCH mice have gut-intrinsic defects in colonic motor behaviors8, suggesting that colonic NOS1 neurons are key androgen targets. To test this, we studied colonic contractions in ex vivo preparations that enable isolation of gut-intrinsic neuronal contributions and can resolve which aspects of motor reflexes are affected (Extended Data Fig. 3a,b). In sum, androgens signal to Nav1.8+ extrinsic neurons and three components of the inhibitory neuromuscular junction in the adult colon: NOS1+ myenteric neurons, SMCs and PDGFRα+ cells. While all these cell types can influence gut motility, androgen signaling is necessary only in the neuronal populations for normal transit, and genetic depletion of AR in NOS1+ neurons alone is sufficient to cause gut-intrinsic defects in colonic motor behaviors.

Microorganisms dynamically affect host androgens Depleting gonadal androgens disrupts motor behaviors in the colon, but not the stomach or small intestine8. The colon has a much greater density of resident bacteria than the upper GI tract, which could explain this difference12. Supporting this possibility, prior studies have shown: (i) the colon has higher DHT levels than the small intestine; (ii) fecal microbial transplants or probiotics can alter serum testosterone levels in recipient mice; (iii) germ-free mice have lower levels of bioavailable androgens in colonic contents than conventionally raised mice13,14,24,25. Thus, bacteria in the colon might generate the androgenic ligands that signal to AR-expressing NOS1+ neurons in the ENS to stimulate colonic motor activity, potentially representing a host–microbe interaction necessary for normal colonic function. To test this hypothesis, we examined the effects of depleting gut microorganisms on GI transit and the host androgen axis. Male CD1 mice were administered a commonly used regimen of broad-spectrum antibiotics (ABX) or vehicle (VEH) in drinking water and GITT was measured in both groups at baseline and day 7 (Fig. 2a).

In the brain, AR signaling plays critical roles in circuits mediating sexually dimorphic behaviors such as mating, aggression and courtship11. In the peripheral nervous system, the roles of androgen signaling beyond sexual function are relatively underexplored. The cellular targets of androgens in the ENS and why this pathway specifically regulates motor activity in the colon remain unclear. The greatest diversity and density of bacteria are found in the colon12 and there is evidence that colonic bacteria affect the androgen axis. Fecal microbial transplants into germ-free mice can alter serum testosterone levels in a sex-dependent manner13,14. In humans, gut bacteria have been identified that can synthesize or catabolize androgens in disease states ranging from prostate cancer to depression15–17. To what extent gut microbial activity regulates the host androgen axis in homeostasis and whether this has any impact on peripheral nervous system function is unknown. Here, we aimed to identify the cells in the colon that mediate the effects of androgens on intestinal motility and to determine if this signaling is modulated by bacterial activity, representing a host–microbe interaction that influences nervous system function.

Results Androgen signaling to the colonic neuromuscular circuit Colonic motor behaviors are a cooperative effort between the ENS and an electrically coupled network of smooth muscle cells (SMCs), interstitial cells of Cajal and PDGFRA-expressing (PDGFRα+) fibroblast-like cells, collectively known as the SIP syncytium18. Some enteric neurons and SMCs are reportedly androgen responsive8,19. To better define which of these cell types might regulate motor behaviors in an androgen-dependent manner, we characterized AR expression in the colons of adult wild-type CD1 mice. In the SIP syncytium, the majority of AR+ cells were PDGFRα+ cells in males and females (Fig. 1a and Extended Data Fig. 1a). AR was also expressed by some SMCs, but never interstitial cells of Cajal (Fig. 1b and Extended Data Fig. 1a,b). The ENS, unlike the SIP syncytium, showed regional variation with AR expression highest in the distal colon (Fig. 1c–e). Although AR expression is robust in the human colonic ENS in males and females8, in mice colonic enteric neurons expressed AR only in males (Fig. 1c–e and Extended Data Fig. 1c), corroborating our previous observations in another genetic background8. Gut-innervating extrinsic neurons, such as visceral afferents, can also modulate colonic motility. AR was robustly expressed by Scn10a+ (encodes Nav1.8) primary afferent neurons located in dorsal root ganglia (DRG) at lumbosacral spinal levels (Fig. 1f). AR was rare to undetectable in vagal afferents or sympathetic neurons in prevertebral ganglia, and weakly expressed by vagal efferents, which have less impact on colonic motility20 (Extended Data Fig. 1d–f). The ENS comprises ~15 types of neurons identified by various neurochemical markers21,22. Motor behaviors are ascribed to polarized circuits in which cholinergic intrinsic primary afferent neurons activate ascending and descending relays of interneurons that ultimately synapse on motor neurons23. Ascending relays activate cholinergic excitatory motor neurons, which stimulate contraction of the proximal gut wall. Descending relays, conversely, activate nitrergic inhibitory motor neurons that stimulate distal relaxation23. We found that virtually all AR+ enteric neurons in the colon expressed NOS1 (Fig. 1g,k), the biosynthetic enzyme for neuronal nitric oxide, and constituted 32% of all NOS1+ neurons in the distal colon (Extended Data Fig. 1g,h). AR immunoreactivity was undetectable in cholinergic neurons marked by Chat (Extended Data Fig. 1i), indicating that androgen signaling is restricted to the inhibitory arm of the peristaltic reflex circuit. Reduced 16S rRNA gene levels in fecal pellets and cecal hypertrophy in ABX mice confirmed effective microbial depletion (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 4a,b). ABX mice at day 7 exhibited markedly slow GI transit (Fig. 2c), as reported with mice on other broad-spectrum ABX regimens1,6,7,26. Spontaneous fecal pellet output (FPO), a measure primarily reflecting colonic motility, was lower in ABX mice than VEH controls (Fig. 2d), and their colons, but not their small intestines, were longer (Extended Data Fig. 4c,d), phenocopying changes observed in ORCH mice8. Remarkably, this short course of ABX was sufficient to dramatically lower serum testosterone levels (Fig. 2e). This deficit was associated with a reduction in the weight of seminal vesicles, an androgen-dependent tissue (Fig. 2f). Serum levels of testosterone negatively correlated with GITT (Fig. 2g), and positively correlated with FPO (Fig. 2h), indicating that the level of circulating androgens could predict colonic motor function. Similarly to ORCH mice (Fig. 1j), ABX mice showed a dramatic loss of AR expression in enteric neurons and

nonneuronal cells (Fig. 2i–k), but not in DRG or the dorsal motor nucleus of the vagus (Extended Data Fig. 4e,f). Previous studies have shown that nitrergic enteric neurons are vulnerable to microbial dysbiosis6,27,28. Consistent with this, we observed fewer NOS1-immunoreactive neurons in ABX mice (Fig. 2l). AR loss could thus represent ligand depletion and/ or loss of NOS1 neurons; the concomitant loss of AR in the SIP syncytium suggests that both are likely (Fig. 2j). Taken together, these findings demonstrate that androgen signaling to the ENS is dependent on gut microorganisms—a short course of enteral ABX was sufficient to reduce host serum testosterone levels, disrupt intestinal motility and abolish AR expression in the ENS. Many bacterial–host interactions are dynamic. To determine if the host responds to microbial depletion with respect to the androgen axis, we studied cohorts of mice exposed to ABX for 21–28 days. Seminal vesicle weight partially recovered by 21 days and returned to baseline by 28 days despite persistent microbial depletion (Extended Data Fig. 4g).

Various microbial metabolites have been reported to regulate host GI motility including aryl hydrocarbon receptor ligands and short-chain fatty acids1,2,4,7,30. Microbial depletion would affect all of these signaling molecules, making it unclear how androgens rank among these factors. To determine to what extent androgens alone would be sufficient to restore dysmotility induced by microbial depletion, we tested the effects of boosting circulating androgen levels on GITTs in ABX mice. Adult male CD1 mice were placed on ABX or VEH, and ABX mice were confirmed to have slowed GI transit at 7 days. Then, mice from each group received subcutaneous implants that continuously released DHT, the nonaromatizable androgen or placebo, while they continued on ABX or VEH in drinking water for 21 more days (Fig. 3c). Compared to placebo, DHT implants increased levels of circulating DHT but did not alter testosterone levels (Fig. 3d and Extended Data Fig. 5e). In VEH mice, this was associated with increased seminal vesicle mass; ABX mice had normal body and seminal vesicle weights and this was unaffected by DHT supplementation (Extended Data Fig. 5f,g). On day 28, which was 21 days after implant placement, all ABX mice had similarly increased cecal mass, signifying equivalent microbial depletion (Extended Data Fig. 5h). When motility was tested, ABX mice implanted with placebo pellets continued to have prolonged transit times at day 28, similar to day 7, while ABX mice implanted with DHT pellets showed partial normalization of their transit times (Fig. 3e) and increased FPO (Fig. 3f). DHT supplementation increased the proportion of AR-immunoreactive neurons in the distal colons of ABX mice, restoring them to similar levels as the VEH groups (Fig. 3g,h and Extended Data Fig. 5i). The overwhelming majority of AR+ neurons in all four groups were NOS1+, indicating that a nitrergic subset of myenteric neurons is faithfully androgen responsive (Extended Data Fig. 5j–l). The robust restoration of AR expression in NOS1+ neurons despite ongoing antibiotic exposure suggested that NOS1 neurons may not necessarily be lost upon dysbiosis. To test this possibility, we genetically labeled Nos1 neurons in Nos1CreER/+Rosa26tdTomato/+ mice and then administered ABX or VEH for 7–21 days. The proportion of labeled tdTomato+ neurons was unchanged by ABX exposure; however, many of these neurons lost NOS1 immunoreactivity by 7 days and this was largely restored by 21 days (Extended Data Fig. 6). Thus, microbial depletion diminishes NOS1 protein expression but does not provoke neuronal loss. Collectively, these data show that robust, postpubertal

levels of circulating androgens are necessary for microbial depletion to cause dysmotility, and that systemic supplementation of DHT is sufficient to restore AR signaling to NOS1 neurons in the ENS to partly rescue this deficit.

Microbial GUS activity regulates androgen signaling in the ENS Host–microbe interactions can be both dynamic and bidirectional. In prostate cancer, for example, castration can stimulate the emergence of bacterial species capable of synthesizing androgens15. In homeostasis, it is unclear how gut bacterial populations are modulated by host androgen levels. To determine this, we performed unbiased shotgun metagenomic sequencing of fecal samples from male CD1 mice longitudinally sampled at three time points: prepubertal (Pre; 3–4 weeks), postpubertal (Post; 6–7 weeks) and 4 weeks after either SHAM or ORCH surgery (Fig. 4a). Principal coordinates analyses revealed minimal taxonomic variance at the genus level between the four groups (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 7a,b). Use of linear discriminant analysis effect size (LEfSe) identified a limited number of species exhibiting differential abundance between prepubertal and postpubertal mice, or SHAM and ORCH mice (Extended Data Fig. 7c,d). Comparing samples from low-androgen conditions (Pre, ORCH) to high-androgen conditions (Post, SHAM) showed the latter to have more Firmicutes (Extended Data Fig. 7e). In contrast to these relatively minor taxonomic differences, there was a marked shift in the functional potential of the fecal microbiome from prepuberty to postpuberty that was not dependent on the continued presence of gonadal androgens in adult mice (Fig. 4b and Extended Data Fig. 7f,g). Thus, at the genetic level, the functional capability of the gut microbiome shifts during male puberty in mice in tandem with the induction of AR expression in the ENS. Microbial GUS enzymes represent one functional capability of the gut microbiome that could shift to affect colonic androgen levels. Circulating steroids are normally glucuronidated and excreted into urine and bile31. Bacterial GUS enzymes cleave the glycosidic bond of steroid glucuronides, regenerating free steroids in the gut lumen32. We found that microbial depletion with 7 days of ABX was sufficient to disrupt GUS activity, leading to elevated levels of androgen glucuronides in the feces of both sexes, and a relative paucity of free DHT in males that was unchanged by systemic DHT supplementation (Extended Data Fig. 8a–c), similar to observations in germ-free mice24. Over 400 unique GUS enzymes have been identified across the mouse gut microbiome, representing 7 different classes of enzymes based on active-site structural features33; these are poorly represented in the Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG). Thus, we used a targeted structural metagenomics pipeline to comprehensively examine GUS gene abundance in the fecal microbial metagenomes of male mice33,34. Across all the samples, 70 representative GUS sequences were observed at 95% identity, spanning 7 classes of GUS enzymes (Extended Data Fig. 8d,e). Hierarchical clustering of GUS gene prevalence showed that the largest difference was between prepubertal and postpubertal mice (Fig. 4c), indicating that the genetic repertoire of microbial GUS shifts with host puberty but is less affected by subsequent depletion of gonadal hormones. GUS gene intensity analysis of fecal metagenomic data from 506 human males similarly revealed that samples from 3–9-year-old boys, presumably prepubertal, segregated from the samples from 18–24-year-old young adults (Fig. 4d,e). Focused analysis of the genes detected in at least 10% of all samples showed that prepubertal males had a broader GUS repertoire (Extended Data Fig. 8f), and identified specific GUS genes enriched in adult males that could be relevant to androgen deconjugation (Fig. 4f). Microbial GUS gene prevalence may not necessarily reflect GUS activity or GUS protein abundance35. To determine if microbial GUS activity changes over developmental time, deglucuronidation of the broad GUS substrate 4-methylumbelliferyl-β-d-glucuronide (4-MUG) was assayed in fimo from fecal samples obtained from independent cohorts of Pre, Post, SHAM and ORCH mice. Mean GUS activity was no different between Pre and Post samples or between SHAM and ORCH samples; however, there was substantially more variation in GUS activity in mice with robust circulating androgen levels, represented by the Post and SHAM groups (Extended Data Fig. 9a–e). Comparing samples from mice in low-androgen states (Pre and ORCH) with those from higher androgen states (Post and SHAM), GUS activity was increased in the high-androgen group (Fig. 4g). This activity was abolished in fecal samples from ABX mice, confirming that in fimo activity measurements reflected microbial rather than host metabolism of glucuronide conjugates (Extended Data Fig. 9f). In sum, fecal microbial GUS activity becomes more variable following puberty and is generally diminished in low-androgen states. To determine if microbial GUS activity is critical for androgen signaling to the ENS, we sought to test whether restoring GUS in the colonic lumen would be sufficient to compensate for the absence of gut microorganisms in ABX mice. To do this, first we needed to identify a microbial GUS that efficiently metabolized androgen glucuronides. GUS enzymes are structurally diverse and utilize a variety of endobiotic and xenobiotic substrates33. Loop 1 GUS enzyme from Escherichia coli has been previously shown to deconjugate estradiol at C17 (ref. 32). Given the similar location of the glucuronide moiety in testosterone and DHT glucuronides (Extended Data Fig. 9g) and E. coli GUS enrichment in the fecal metagenomes of postpubertal males (Fig. 4f), we reasoned that this GUS might reactivate androgens. E. coli GUS activity was tested in vitro with testosterone and DHT glucuronide substrates and the resulting products, testosterone and DHT, were quantified by liquid chromatography coupled to tandem mass spectrometry (LC–MS/MS) or gas chromatography. E. coli GUS cleaved testosterone glucuronide at a rate of 0.033 µM s−1 ± 0.001 and DHT glucuronide to a similar extent (Fig. 4h and Extended Data Fig. 9h–j), comparable to previous observations for estrogens32. To assess if GUS activity in the colonic lumen could rescue the effects of microbial depletion on the androgen–ENS axis, adult male mice were again administered ABX or VEH for 7 days and either recombinant E. coli GUS or a heat-inactivated control once daily per rectum starting on day 3 (Fig. 4i–l and Extended Data Fig. 10). Given that rectal infusions have cathartic effects, we could not utilize intestinal transit

as a readout. Instead, we assessed AR immunoreactivity in the ENS because it was consistently linked with intestinal motility in ABX mice (Figs. 1i–m, 2c–k and 3e–h). ABX mice administered inactivated E. coli GUS had no AR expression in the ENS (Fig. 4k); in contrast, administration of active E. coli GUS restored AR and NOS1 expression in enteric neurons (Fig. 4l–n). Notably, both groups of ABX mice had reduced serum testosterone levels and seminal vesicle weights compared to VEH controls (Fig. 4o,p). These observations indicate that when gut microorganisms are depleted, introduction of a single E. coli GUS into the colonic lumen is sufficient to restore AR expression in NOS1+ myenteric neurons without altering systemic androgens, suggesting that the ENS depends on microbial GUS activity.

Discussion Altogether, our observations show that dynamic and bidirectional host–microbe interactions involving androgen metabolism are necessary for neural regulation of intestinal motility. Inactive host androgen glucuronides excreted into the gut lumen become substrates for microbial GUS enzymes, which cleave off the glucuronide moieties to generate a potent pool of active androgens. These reactivated androgens signal to enteric neurons to stimulate motility while also being reabsorbed into the systemic circulation. Recycled androgens constitute such a substantial part of the host’s circulating levels that microbial disruption with a short course of broad-spectrum ABX causes symptomatic hypogonadism. With continued antibiotic exposure, the host eventually compensates and restores normal circulating levels of testosterone. This compensation is not sufficient to restore AR expression in the colonic ENS or normalize intestinal motility, suggesting that the ENS is particularly dependent on local microbial androgen synthesis. In turn, fecal microbial GUS composition shifts with puberty in male mice and humans, becoming enriched for a GUS that efficiently reactivates androgens. Gut motor behaviors vary along the intestine in variety, complexity and extent of neuronal regulation36,37. We previously found that gonadal androgens were selectively required for colonic motor function8. Multiple nonneural and neural cell types involved in colonic motility express AR but conditional deletion only in Nav1.8+ or NOS1+ neurons was sufficient to slow transit. The ~33% slowing of transit in each of these receptor knockouts combines to approach the larger effect observed upon depletion of gonadal androgens by orchiectomy, suggesting that androgen signaling to both neuronal populations is likely important in homeostasis. Within the ENS, virtually all AR+ cells were NOS1+ motor neurons, which inhibit smooth muscle contraction in a regulated manner to enable propulsive activity. ARNOS1KO mice exhibited gut-intrinsic defects in this coordinated relaxation that resembled those reported in ORCH mice8, indicating that androgen signaling to NOS1 neurons is necessary for normal colonic contractility. The AR-dependent mechanisms within Nav1.8+ and NOS1+ neurons that mediate these motor effects and the functional significance of androgen signaling in AR+ nonneural cells remain to be defined. Mice, rats and humans have markedly higher androgen levels in the colon than the serum24,38, leading to our hypothesis that the ENS responds to this local source of ligand. Colonic testosterone and DHT levels are low in germ-free mice, suggesting that microorganisms are involved in their production24. Seminal studies established that transplantation of gut microorganisms or feces into germ-free or conventionally raised mice could alter serum testosterone levels in mice13,14, but the data have been conflicting on whether microorganisms are necessary for normal systemic androgen levels13,14,24,39. We found that microbial depletion by exposure to broad-spectrum ABX for 7 days was sufficient to drop circulating levels of androgens, induce atrophy of androgen-dependent tissues, abolish AR expression in the ENS and slow intestinal motility. These observations establish that the androgen axis in postpubertal male mice depends on microbial activity. Studies using microbial depletion as a tool should consider effects on this axis.

Broad-spectrum ABX are routinely used in clinical practice and often associated with altered bowel habits—androgen deficits may have a role in these adverse effects. With prolonged microbial depletion, the host axis compensated with recovery of systemic, but not fecal, levels of androgens. This compensatory response, however, was insufficient to fully restore AR expression in the ENS or normalize transit. This observation may reflect the tissue specificity of androgen effects that have been recently reported40,41, or that ENS androgen signaling depends on local production of androgens in the colon. Boosting circulating DHT to supraphysiologic levels in mice on ABX was sufficient to restore AR expression in enteric NOS1 neurons and partly normalize motility, indicating that the ENS requires particularly high levels of androgenic ligands that are probably normally derived locally. The ready restoration of AR+ NOS1+ neurons upon systemic DHT or rectal E. coli GUS administration seemed at odds with our observations and previous reports of enteric NOS1 neuron loss upon microbial disruption6,27,28. Genetic labeling of NOS1 neurons, however, revealed that microbial depletion does not provoke neuronal loss but reduces NOS1 expression, limiting the number that are detected by immunohistochemistry. Although administering colonic GUS activity was sufficient to restore both NOS1 and AR expression in the ENS, ARNOS1KO and ORCH mice showed normal numbers of NOS1+ neurons, indicating that androgens signal through NOS1+ neurons but are not necessary for NOS1 expression. Mouse fecal metagenomics showed that the functional genetic potential of the microbiome shifts with puberty. Dedicated analysis of GUS gene abundance highlighted this group of enzymes as among those that shift over this period in both mice and humans. Hundreds of unique GUS enzymes have been identified in the mouse and human microbiomes, which can be classified into at least seven categories based on functional active sites33,34. Metagenomic analysis of human fecal samples identified E. coli Loop 1 GUS as highly enriched in postpubertal males. This enzyme efficiently liberated glucuronidated androgens and local colonic administration was sufficient to restore AR expression in the ENS in mice on ABX. While our studies focused on male mice, we found that microbial depletion also affected fecal androgen and estrogen levels in females. The human female ENS expresses receptors for both42. Estrogens can slow intestinal transit and were previously identified as E. coli GUS substrates32. Microbial GUS activity thus likely impacts neural regulation of intestinal motility in both sexes, with potentially opposing effects of androgens and estrogens in females. Identification of additional microbial GUS proteins capable of reactivating androgens and the structural features that confer substrate specificity will be important to advance the understanding of the many human diseases in which these steroid hormones are implicated and may enable selective modulation of peripheral neural circuits.

Methods Animals Mice were housed in a specific pathogen-free facility with a 12-h dark cycle and handled per protocols (18-12-3841, 00001526 and 00002432) approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee of Boston Children’s Hospital that were adherent to the National Institutes of Health (NIH) Guide for the Care and Use of Laboratory Animals. All wild-type mice in this study were outbred CD1 mice purchased from ENVIGO. Postpubertal mice weighed ≥30 g and prepubertal mice were studied following weaning and weighed <20 g. All transgenic mouse strains are listed in Supplementary Table 1 and were maintained on a C57BL/6 background. To generate male AR conditional knockout mice, males heterozygous for the Cre knockin allele (NOS1CreER/+, PDGFRaCreERT2/+, SM22aCreERT2/+, Nav1.8Cre/+) were bred with homozygous ARfl/fl females to generate NOS1CreER/+ ARfl/Y mice (ARNOS1KO), PDGFRαCreER/+ ARfl/Y mice (ARPDGFRαKO), SM22CreER/+ ARfl/Y mice (ARSM22KO) and Nav1.8Cre/+ ARfl/Y mice (ARNav1.8KO). To generate female AR conditional knockout mice, ARPDGFRαKO and ARSM22KO males were bred with homozygous ARfl/fl females to generate PDGFRαCreER/+ ARfl/fl and SM22CreER/+ ARfl/fl mice, respectively. Cre-negative ARfl/Y or ARfl/fl littermate controls were used in all experiments and induced with tamoxifen in parallel. All conditional knockout mice were born at expected Mendelian ratios, had similar body weights to ARfl/Y or ARfl/fl littermates and were well-appearing. Cre-expressing lines were first validated by breeding with Rosa26Ai9/Ai9 females to generate mice heterozygous for Cre and the Ai9 transgene, which encodes a Cre-dependent tdTomato reporter. For both Cre validation and KO studies, mice were administered 2 mg of tamoxifen by orogastric gavage once daily for 2 days at 6 weeks of age to induce Cre activity. Body weights were recorded before tamoxifen induction and 7 days after tamoxifen induction. All animal experiments represent observations from at least two independent cohorts. All mice were analyzed at 7–14 weeks of age, except where prepubertal mice are specifically studied, as described above.

Antibiotic administration Body weight and GITT were measured at baseline, before initiating ABX or VEH exposure. For ABX, 1 g l−1 ampicillin, 1 g l−1 neomycin, 0.5 g l−1 vancomycin, 0.3 g l−1 metronidazole and 1% Splenda (to promote palatability) were dissolved in sterile, autoclaved water. For VEH, mice received 1% Splenda dissolved in sterile, autoclaved water. Mice were allowed to drink ABX or VEH water ad libitum for the duration of the experiment. Body weights were assessed every 3–4 days to ensure adequate hydration and that they did not drop below 20% from baseline. Water bottles were replaced one to two times per week. Intestinal transit was followed longitudinally in the experimental cohorts.

Measurement of EUB 16S Stool was collected from mice on days 0, 7, 21 and 28 of antibiotic treatment. DNA was extracted from stool according to the protocol as stated (Qiagen, 51604) and stored at −30 °C until use. Quantitative PCR was performed with SYBR Green Master Mix (Thermo Fisher, A25776). Genomic DNA was measured using a Nano-drop One. Primers are EUB16S F: GGTGAATACGTTCCCGG; EUB16S R: TACGGCTACCTTGT TACGA15. Data were normalized to average of the VEH group and 2−Delta CT was used to calculate 16S gene abundance per gram of feces.

Orchiectomy and sham surgical procedures Approximately 6-week-old male CD1 male mice (25–30 g, Envigo) were anesthetized with 3% inhalable isoflurane (Isospire, ANADA 200-129) and then administered ophthalmic eye ointment (Dechra NDC 17033- 211-38), 10 mg per kg body weight subcutaneous meloxicam (Putney NDC 26637-621-01) and subcutaneous bupivacaine at the incision site (MWI Veterinary Supply, Boise, ID; 0.25%, 2–3 mg per kg body weight diluted with 50% saline for final 0.125% solution). Fur was removed from

the scrotum using clippers, and the surgical area was sterilized with chlorhexidine and 70% ethanol. Using sterile technique, a single incision was made on the midline of the scrotum. Blunt forceps were used to grasp one testicular fat pad, and a ligature of absorbable suture material was placed around the epididymis. Using sharp scissors, the testicle was removed, and the remaining tissue returned to the scrotal sac. Using the same incision, the procedure was repeated to excise the second testicle. After ensuring adequate bleeding control, the skin was closed with simple interrupted nonabsorbable sutures. For sham operation, the same scrotal incision was made, the testicles were visualized and then testes were returned to the scrotal sac followed by skin closure as above. All animals received meloxicam 24 h after the first injections to minimize postoperative pain. CD1 ORCH and SHAM mice were indistinguishable in their cages, with seminal vesicle weight, noted to be lower in ORCH mice, confirming the efficiency of androgen depletion.

DHT subcutaneous implant procedure Mice were anesthetized and provided with periprocedural bupivacaine and meloxicam analgesia, as described above. Pellets containing DHT or placebo (Innovative Research of America, SA-161 or SC-111, respectively) were implanted subcutaneously under sterile conditions between the shoulder blades. The pellets contained 7.5 mg DHT/ placebo and were designed to continuously release 0.125 mg per day of DHT over 60 days. No post-procedure analgesia was administered, as advised by veterinary consultation.

Nitric oxide synthase activity assay Colons were dissected, washed and then the distal 3-cm segment was isolated. The segments were then mechanically stripped to remove the mucosa from the muscle layers, retaining the portion containing the submucosal plexus, circular muscle, myenteric plexus and longitudinal muscle. This tissue fragment was then snap frozen in liquid nitrogen and stored at −80 °C until use. Tissue was prepared and the assay run according to the manufacturer’s protocol (Abcam, ab211083). Results were normalized to protein concentration in each tissue homogenate, determined by a Pierce BCA protein assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific, 23225)

Immunohistochemistry and quantification Gut tissues were isolated and immunostaining performed as previously described43. For AR staining, whole mounts were fixed for 1 h in 4% paraformaldehyde (PFA)/PBS. For dorsal root, nodose and sympathetic ganglia, tissues were fixed in 4% PFA/PBS for 1 h at 4 °C, rinsed twice in PBS, washed 6 × 20 min with PBST (PBS + 0.5% Triton), incubated in primary antibody diluted in blocking solution (PBST + 20% dimethylsulfoxide (DMSO) + 5% NDS) at room temperature for 48–72 h, washed 6 × 20 min with PBST, incubated in secondary antibody at room temperature for 24 h, washed 6 × 20 min with PBST, then rinsed with PBS. Tissues were mounted onto glass slides with a coverslip. For mouse brain, tissue was fixed in 4% PFA/PBS overnight at 4 °C, then rinsed twice in PBS. Samples were embedded in 4% agarose gel in PBS and 100-μm sections were obtained using a vibratome. The sections were washed and stained as described above and then mounted onto slides with a coverslip for imaging. Nuclei were counterstained with DAPI in Vectashield mounting medium (Vector Labs H-1200). To quantify AR+ neurons, 1.5-cm segments of the colon were immunostained as whole mounts for ANNA-1, AR and NOS1. Single planar images were captured at the level of the myenteric plexus (six fields per segment, identified based on ANNA-1 signal alone). All whole mounts were imaged on a Zeiss LSM 880 confocal microscope using Airyscan settings or a Leica Sp8. To quantify NOS1+ and TdTomato+ neurons in Nos1CreER/+ Rosa26tdTomato/+ mice, 1.5-cm segments of the colon were immunostained as whole mounts for ANNA-1 and NOS1 and imaged on a Zeiss LSM 700 confocal microscope to capture z-stacks at the level of the myenteric plexus (six fields per segment, identified based on ANNA-1 signal alone). Neurons counted from all six fields per animal were summed to arrive at our measurements of the percentage of all colonic neurons in an intestinal segment per animal that were AR+ or NOS1+. To quantify AR+ neurons in the DRG, whole mounts were imaged on a Zeiss LSM 700 confocal microscope to capture z-stacks that included all neurons in the ganglion (4–6 fields per ganglion, identified based on TUBB3 signal alone). For all the above quantifications, images were coded, randomized and quantified using ImageJ by investigators blinded to the experimental condition.

GI motility and stool composition analyses Total GITT was measured as previously described43. In brief, mice were placed into clean cages with food and water but no bedding. At 8:50, mice were administered 300 µl of 6% carmine red in 0.5% methylcellulose by oral gavage. After 30–60 min, cages were checked every 10 min for fecal pellets containing red dye. All knockout mice and controls were assessed at 60 min after gavage. We observed CD1 mice to have faster baseline motility and thus their fecal pellets were checked starting at 30 min after gavage. FPO represents the number of pellets spontaneously excreted by each animal over a 30–60-min period, as specified in corresponding graphs and figure legends. For ex vivo imaging of colonic motility, the entire colon distal to the cecum was acutely isolated from each mouse and cannulated in an organ bath maintained at 37 °C containing continuously oxygenated Krebs solution (see schematic in Extended Data Fig. 3a). The organ bath accommodates two colons, and colons from experimental and control mice were studied in tandem in every recording session. Intraluminal pressure was kept consistent between both colons and across experiments by regulating fluid column heights leading to both cannulae. After a 15-min equilibration period, colonic contractile activity was video recorded and analyzed using Scribble and MATLAB scripts, as previously described8. In brief, this analysis generates spatiotemporal heat maps from each 15-min video in which color represents gut width (degree of contraction), the x axis represents the proximal-to-distal

length of the colon, and the y axis represents time. Colonic migrating motor contractions were defined as contractions that originated in the proximal colon and successfully propagated at least 50% of the length of the tissue. To determine the rate and time required for relaxation of individual colonic migrating motor contractions, vertical slice analysis was performed at two positions along the x axis of the heat map: one at one-third of the length of the colon (proximal slice) and one at two-thirds of the length (distal slice). This generates line graphs at these two points showing gut width over time. From these graphs, the rate of relaxation was calculated from determining the change in gut width over the change in time as averaged from two contractions per video. Fifteen-minute videos were recorded and analyzed for each mouse (22 videos from 8 CTRL mice; 21 videos from 7 KO littermates).

Serum testosterone measurements by ELISA For testosterone analysis by ELISA, blood was allowed to coagulate for 30 min following collection and centrifuged for 10 min at 2,500g at room temperature. Resulting serum was divided into 100-μl aliquots per animal and stored at −80 °C until use. To extract steroids, samples were thawed at room temperature, suspended in 3:1 ethyl acetate:sample ratio, vortexed thoroughly for 15 min at room temperature and then centrifuged for 3 min at 2,000g at room temperature. Supernatants were collected into new 1.5-ml tubes and the process was repeated once more. The final steroid supernatant containing ethyl acetate was evaporated in a speed vacuum for 30 min at 35 °C and then stored at −80 °C until use. For testosterone ELISA (Cayman Chemicals, 582701), samples were reconstituted in 300 μl ELISA buffer (Cayman Chemicals, 582701) and the manufacturer’s protocol was used. Plates were read on a TECAN at 405 nm and 420 nm at 60 min and 90 min. Analysis was performed on the 420-nm reading at 60–90 min, according to kit instructions, and a standard curve was generated using GraphPad Prism. If sample concentration was less than 100 µl, final values were divided by serum volume.

Recombinant E. coli GUS colonic infusions Five thousand units of recombinant E. coli GUS (Sigma, G7646-5KU) were dissolved in 2 ml of sterile water such that one dose of enzyme administered was equal to 80 µl, ~200 units of enzyme. Control enzyme was heat inactivated for 30 min at 75 °C. CD1 mice were placed on ABX or VEH, as described above, for 7 days. Starting on day 3 (72 h after ABX or VEH onset), mice were briefly anesthetized with 3% inhalable isoflurane (Isospire, ANADA 200-129) and a soft-tipped, plastic flexible feeding needle (Instech, 20‑gauge, 38 mm, 50-810-47) was inserted 2 cm into each rectum. One dose (80 µl) of either recombinant enzyme or heat-inactivated enzyme was slowly infused into the colon, and then the needle was removed. Mice were removed from anesthesia and held at a 45° angle head down for a few minutes to ensure no leakage of solution. This procedure was repeated three more times for a total of four doses in 4 days. On day 7, mice were euthanized, and tissue was collected.

Shotgun metagenomics of mouse fecal samples Sixteen CD1 mice weighing 12–14 g were separated into four cages upon arrival. Stool samples were collected from mice before puberty (<20 g) and after puberty (>30 g mice with palpable testes). Mice were then separated into two groups and underwent SHAM or ORCH surgeries (eight mice per group). ORCH and SHAM stool collection was obtained 4 weeks after surgery. All fecal samples were frozen at −80 °C until use. Fecal samples were shipped to EzBiome (Gaithersburg) for DNA extraction, library preparation, sequencing and preliminary bioinformatic analysis. Genomic DNA was prepared using the ZymoBIOMICS DNA Miniprep Kit (Zymo Research) with a final elution volume of 50 μl. Concentration of double-stranded DNA was measured using an Invitrogen Qubit 4.0 Fluorometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Sequencing libraries were prepared using a NEBNext Ultra II FS Library Prep Kit for Illumina (New England Biolabs) sequencing, using the HiSeq 4000

Gut microbial GUS gene analyses Procurement of human metagenomic samples. Metagenomic sequencing data from 506 human samples from healthy males aged 3–9 (N = 278) or 18–24 years old (N = 228) were obtained from publicly accessible studies curated by EzBiome. The metadata and accession numbers for these samples are included in Supplementary Table 3.

Initial processing of mouse and human metagenomic samples. Each metagenomic sample was processed through the workflow shown in Supplementary Fig. 1. Raw metagenomic reads were trimmed, filtered and assembled de novo into open reading frames (ORFs), using NGLess (v1.4.2) with default parameters46. Generic feature format files and predicted protein sequences were generated from the ORFs using Prodigal (v2.6.3)47.

Identification and characterization of GUS gene sequences from mouse and human fecal metagenomic data. Metagenomic amino acid sequences were clustered to remove redundancies using CD-HIT (v4.8.1) at a sequence identity threshold of 100%. These representative protein sequences were then used to identify putative GUS enzymes as reported previously34,35. Accepted sequences were clustered again at 95% using CD-HIT, forming a representative set of GUS sequences for downstream analysis48. Representative sequences were aligned to reference sequences from each loop class in a multiple sequence alignment using Clustal Omega, and GUS class was assigned according to parameters reported previously34,35,49. Taxonomy was assigned to representative GUS sequences with a lowest common ancestor algorithm, using Diamond (v2.0.15.153) to map GUS representatives to proteins in the CMMG and UHGP, for mouse and human gut metagenomes, respectively34,50–53. Phylogenetic inference was performed on representative GUS sequences using Muscle5 (v5.1)54 and IQ-TREE 2 (v2.2.0.3)55. The resulting Newick tree file was combined with the GUS class and taxonomic annotations to create a cladogram (Extended Data Fig. 7) using ggtree (v3.2.1) and ggplot2 in R (v4.1.2)56,57.

Metagenomic gene intensity quantification. For each sample, a bowtie2 index was created from the ORFs. A SAM file was then created by aligning the trimmed and filtered reads to the bowtie2 index. The SAM and generic feature format files were used to generate gene read counts in each sample, using featureCounts from the package SUB- READ (v2.0.1)58. Gene read counts for all samples were then normalized based on the total reads detected in each sample and in all samples, yielding normalized intensity of each gene’s read count. These gene intensities were then filtered to only the representative GUS sequences. GUS gene intensities were further normalized to correct for the association between gene length and gene intensity. These methods were implemented exactly as reported in previous work35,47.

GUS gene intensity analysis. To visualize the associations between GUS gene intensities and study groups, heat maps (Fig. 4c,e) were created from GUS gene intensities using the ‘splsda’ and ‘cim’ functions in mixOmics (v6.18.1). The GUS class composition of the GUS genes identified in each mouse study group (Extended Data Fig. 8d,e) was calculated by dividing the unique count of GUS representatives of a given class present in a study group by the total unique count of GUS genes present in that study group. To visualize the associations between GUS gene intensities and human study groups, a sparse partial least squares regression discriminant analysis sample plot (Fig. 4d) was created from GUS gene intensities using the ‘splsda’ and ‘plotIndiv’ functions in mixOmics. Differential abundance analysis was performed

on human metagenomic GUS genes summed at 95% identity using the Kruskal–Wallis test in R (Fig. 4f and Supplementary Table 2). Human metagenomic GUS genes present in ≥10% of all samples were visualized using pheatmap (v1.0.12) in R (Extended Data Fig. 8f).

In fimo analyses of GUS activity (related to Fig. 4g and Extended Data Fig. 9a–f) Approximately 1–5 pellets per mouse were thawed on ice and added to 350–750 µl resuspension buffer (25 mM HEPES, 25 mM NaCl pH 7.4 with one Roche Complete protease inhibitor tablet), depending on the amount of fecal material, and 1 g autoclaved garnet beads in 2-ml screw-cap tubes. The mixture was vortexed on high for 1 min and were beaten on a Qiagen Tissuelyzer II at 30 Hz for 2 min. The tubes were sonicated for 2 min in a 4 °C water bath, shaken, sonicated again and then centrifuged at 13,000g for 10 min at 4 °C. The resulting supernatants were filtered by centrifugation for 10 min at 13,000g in a 1.5-ml Amicon 10-kDa cutoff spin concentrator. The remaining supernatant was mixed and washed with ~250 µl of resuspension buffer by centrifugation at 13,000 g for 10 min at 4 °C. The mixture was then transferred to a new 1.7-ml microcentrifuge tube. The total protein concentration was determined using the Pierce BCA Protein Assay kit using E. coli GUS for the standard. The fecal lysate was diluted to 1 mg ml−1 and snap frozen in small aliquots (each considered a biological replicate). GUS activity of the fecal lysate was determined by measuring hydrolysis of 4-MUG, a fluorescent reporter substrate. 4-MUG was resuspended in DMSO at 50 mM and then diluted to 1 mM in water. Reactions were carried out in black polystyrene half-area Costar 96-well plates with clear, flat bottoms. Total reaction volume was 50 µl and consisted of 35 µl of double-distilled water (ddH2O), 5 µl 10× buffer (250 mM HEPES, 250 mM NaCl, pH 6.5), and 5 µl of fecal lysate at 1 mg ml−1 that were mixed and incubated at 37 °C for 5 min before the reaction was initiated by the addition of 5 µl of 1 mM 4-MUG. Reactions were monitored continuously with an excitation wavelength of 350 nm and an emission wavelength of 450 nm using a CLARIOstar microplate reader. A custom script (available at https://github.com/redinbolab/iterative_linear_fit_notebook/) was used to fit the resulting curve by linear regression to obtain initial velocities. Rates for each biological replicate are the average of three technical replicates ±s.e.m.

In vitro analysis of GUS activity (related to Extended Data Fig. 10b) GUS activity of recombinant E. coli GUS (Sigma, G7646-5KU) or heat-inactivated control (75 °C for 30 min) was determined by measuring hydrolysis of 4-MUG, a fluorescent reporter substrate. 4-MUG was resuspended in DMSO at 50 mM and then diluted to 1 mM in water. Reactions were carried out in black polystyrene half-area Costar 96-well plates with clear, flat bottoms. Total reaction volume was 50 µl and consisted of 35 µl of ddH2O, 5 µl 10× buffer (250 mM HEPES, 250 mM NaCl, pH 6.5) and 5 µl of recombinant E. coli GUS (2.5 units per µl solution) or heat-inactivated enzyme that was mixed and incubated at 37 °C for 5 min before the reaction was initiated by the addition of 5 µl of 1 mM 4-MUG. Reactions were monitored continuously with an excitation wavelength of 350 nm and an emission wavelength of 450 nm using a TECAN microplate reader. Total GUS activity for each biological replicate is the average of three technical replicates ± s.e.m.

In vitro E. coli GUS ± testosterone/DHT turnover assays (related to Fig. 4h and Extended Data Fig. 9h–j) E. coli GUS cleavage of testosterone glucuronide. Reactions contained 37.5 µl of buffer (50 mM HEPES, 50 mM NaCl, pH 6.5) and 2.5 µl E. coli GUS at 100 nM that were incubated at 37 °C for 5 min. The reaction was initiated by the addition of 10 µl testosterone glucuronide at 500 µM

Control reactions contained enzyme that had been heat killed at 90 °C for 5 min. Testosterone quantification via LC–MS/MS. Testosterone production was analyzed with a Waters Acquity Classic UPLC system equipped with an Acquity Premier CSH C18 column (2.1 × 100 mm, 1.7-µm particle size) coupled with a Thermo Scientific TSQ Vantage Ultra Triple Quad mass spectrometer. HPLC tubes were stored in an autosampler at 10 °C before separation on the column, which was maintained at 40 °C. Analytes were separated using a water–methanol gradient. Solvent A is ddH2O with 5 mM ammonium acetate and 0.012% formic acid; solvent B is methanol with 5 mM ammonium acetate and 0.012% formic acid. The LC flow gradient was as follows: 0 min, 50% B; 3 min, 70% B; 4 min, 99% B; 5 min, 99% B; 6 min, 50% B; 7.5 min, 10% B; and 8 min, 50% B. Analytes were separated with a flow rate of 0.3 ml min−1 and an injection volume of 3 µl. Data acquisition was performed by selected reaction monitoring using electrospray ionization in positive ionization mode. The selected reaction monitoring transitions used along with their corresponding collision energies (V) were as follows: 289.16 → 97.07 (25 V) and 289.16 → 109.1 (27 V) for testosterone and 292.1 → 79.07 (37 V), 292.1 → 97.08 (21 V) and 292.1 → 109.09 (26 V) for testosterone-d3. The spray voltage was 3,300 V. Sheath gas pressure was 45 (arbitrary units) and auxiliary gas pressure was 25 (arbitrary units). Concentrations of the analyte were determined using a standard curve of testosterone (Steraloids, A6950-000) with nine points (1.875-60 µM) containing 10 µl of 0.001 mg ml−1 internal standard (testosterone-d3). The data were analyzed using Thermo Xcalibur Quan Browser software (version 3.0.63) and an example chromatogram is shown in Extended Data Fig. 9i.

E. coli GUS cleavage of DHT glucuronide. DHT glucuronide (Steraloids, A2585-000) was resuspended in DMSO at 10 mM and diluted to 500 µM in water. Reactions contained 35 µl of buffer (50 mM HEPES, 50 mM NaCl, pH 6.5) and 5 µl E. coli GUS at 50 nM that were incubated at 37 °C for 5 min. The reaction was initiated by the addition of 10 µl DHT glucuronide at 500 µM yielding an assay concentration of 100 µM. Over the course of 12 min at five time points, 40 µl of 0.2 M sodium carbonate was added to quench the reaction. Control reactions contained enzyme that had been heat-killed at 90 °C for 5 min. Ten microliters of 500 µM internal standard (androsterone, Sigma-Aldrich, 31579) was added to the quenched reactions. The reactions were transferred into 1.7-ml microcentrifuge tubes where they were flash frozen in liquid nitrogen. The samples were then lyophilized for 2 h. Once dry, each reaction was reconstituted with 100 µl of LC–MS-grade acetonitrile and centrifuged at 13,000g for 10 min. The supernatant was then transferred to HPLC tubes and quantified via the detection of DHT by the gas chromatography coupled to mass spectrometry (GC–MS) protocol. Reaction curves for DHT production rates were fit using linear regression. The final turnover value is the average of n = 3 biological replicates ± s.e.m. (Extended Data Fig. 9h).

Quantification of DHT by GC–MS. DHT production was analyzed with a Q Exactive GC Orbitrap GC–MS with a TriPlus RSH Autosampler. Gas chromatography was performed using a Thermo TraceGOLD TG-5SilMS column (30 m × 0.25 m × 0.25 µm). Analytes were separated using a 13-min temperature gradient. The oven holds at 100 °C for

1.5 min before it ramps up at a rate of 30 °C per minute until it reaches 300 °C by minute 8. The oven temperature remains at 300 °C until the protocol ends at minute 13. The prep-run timeout is set to 10 min and the equilibration time is 0.5 min. A splitless method was utilized with 10-µl injections using helium as the carrier gas (constant flow 1.5 ml min−1). The inlet temperature and MS transfer line was 280 °C, while the ion source as 230 °C. The AGC target was set to 1 × 106. A 3.25-min filament delay was used. Data were acquired in positive mode in a full SCAN mode with the range of 40 m/z to 500 m/z and a resolution of 60,000. The retention time for DHT was 9.29 and the retention time for the internal standard, androsterone, was 9.07 (Extended Data Fig. 9j). The data were analyzed using Thermo Xcalibur Quan Browser software (version 3.0.63).

Quantification of androgens in mouse serum and feces by LC–MS/MS for antibiotic experiments (related to Fig. 3d and Extended Data Figs. 5e and 8a–c) All the chemicals used were of high purity suitable for HPLC. Methanol, 1-chlorobutane, dichloromethane, acetonitrile, acetone, ethyl acetate and formic acid were sourced from VWR Canlab. DHT and testosterone (T) were purchased from Steraloids. For stable isotope internal standards (IS), we used dihydrotestosterone (d3-DHT), and testosterone-d3 (d3-T), which were acquired from CDN isotopes. All other chemicals were from Sigma. All initial solutions were made with a concentration of 100 μg ml−1 for each compound by dissolving them in reagent alcohol. These solutions were then frozen at −20 °C. To create working solutions for each steroid, we diluted the stock solutions with an appropriate volume of reagent alcohol and stored these at −20 °C. To establish the calibration standards, we prepared samples in the specific matrix needed (serum charcoal-stripped). These standards covered a range of concentrations: from 2.0 pg ml−1 to 10,000 pg ml−1 for T, and from 5.0 pg ml−1 to 2,000 pg ml−1 for DHT. For blood measurements, 250 μl of plasma was combined with 1 ml of 0.15 M ammonium acetate buffer at pH 4.6, along with 25 μl of a solution containing 20 mg ml−1 of ascorbic acid in water and 50 μl of the internal standard. To this mixture, 3 ml of 1-chlorobutane was added and vigorously vortexed for 2 min and centrifuged at 2,400g for 10 min. Following centrifugation, the organic layer was carefully collected and evaporated under nitrogen at 35 °C for 30 min using a Turbo Vap instrument (Zymark Corporation) before proceeding with derivatization. The residue was diluted with a 0.1 M sodium bicarbonate buffer, its pH adjusted to 9 using ammonium hydroxide, resulting in a final volume of 100 μl. Subsequently, 200 μl of a dansyl chloride solution (1 mg ml−1 in acetone) was quickly mixed with the sample for 10 s. The samples were then heated at 60 °C for 10 min. Next, a mixture of water and methanol (in a ratio of 80:20, vol/vol) amounting to 3 ml was added, and this mixture was loaded onto Strata X 30 mg SPE columns from Phenomenex. Following loading, the columns were washed first with water and then with a mixture of water and methanol (in a ratio of 50:50, vol/vol). DHT and T were subsequently eluted using a mixture of water and methanol (in a ratio of 10:90, vol/vol), while a new set of tubes was used to collect the eluate. The eluates were then evaporated to dryness at 45 °C under a flow of nitrogen gas. DHT and T were reconstituted in a 50:50 mixture of water and methanol, resulting in a final volume of 100 μl. Finally, samples were injected into an LC–MS/MS system for analysis. For measuring glucuronides, 250 μl of a freshly prepared solution of GUS (E. coli type VII A 500 U ml−1) in phosphate buffer (pH 6.5), along with 25 μl of the ascorbic acid solution and 50 μl of internal standard, were added to both the calibration curve and plasma samples (250 μl). The mixture was then incubated for a total of 20 h at 37 °C. Then, 3 ml of 1-chlorobutane was added, and the subsequent steps mirrored those described above for plasma before LC–MS/MS analysis. For fecal samples, 20 mg of lyophilized feces sample was homogenized with 100 mg of stainless-steel beads (0.9–2 mm) and 1 ml of PBS using a bullet blender (Next Advance). LC–MS/MS analysis of plasma and fecal samples consisted of a chromatographic separation accomplished using an HPLC system at room temperature on a Nexera system (Shimadzu Scientific Instruments). Separation occurred on a Supelco Ascentis Express C18 column (150 × 3.0-mm internal diameter, particle size, 2.7 μm) sourced (Sigma) with a total runtime of 23 min. A binary mobile phase was used, composed of 0.1% (vol/vol) formic acid in H2O (designated as solvent A) and 0.1% (vol/vol) formic acid in methanol (designated as solvent B), flowing at a rate of 0.8 ml min−1. The mass spectrometry analytical procedures were conducted using a Sciex mass spectrometer 6500 triple quadrupole system (Sciex). This system was equipped with a turbo ion-spray source and configured to operate in the multiple reaction monitoring mode. System control and data analysis were managed through Analyst 1.6.2 Sciex software. For the analysis of T and DHT, the multiple reaction monitoring transitions used were as follows: 289.1 → 97.2 for T, 291.1 → 255.3 for DHT, 292.1 → 97.2 for d3-T, and 294.1 → 258.3 for d3-DHT. Unit mass resolution was applied in both the masses resolving quadrupole Q1 and Q3. Electrospray ionization was conducted in the positive mode with an ionization voltage of 5,500 V, a declustering potential of 110 V, and a heater probe temperature set at 500 °C. The nebulization and collision gas settings were 70 and medium, respectively. The detection limits for T and DHT were determined to be 2.0 pg ml−1 and 5.0 pg ml−1, respectively.

Statistics and reproducibility No statistical method was used to predetermine sample size. Data were checked for normal distribution, and power analyses were performed before statistical analyses. Outliers were excluded using ROUT’s test. Error bars are displayed as ±s.e.m. n represents an animal, unless otherwise noted. The levels of significance are: *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001 and ****P < 0.0001. For comparison of means from two groups, Levene’s test (F statistic) was first examined to check for equal variances between groups. If variances were equal, an unpaired two-sided Student’s t-test was used. If variances were unequal, Welch’s t-test was used. For comparison of three or more groups, the Brown– Forsythe test (F statistic) was first used to check for equal variances between groups. If variances were not equal, Brown–Forsythe and Welch ANOVA tests were used. If variances were equal, ANOVA was used and post hoc Tukey’s or Sidak’s tests were performed. For repeated measures over time between two groups, two-way ANOVA with multiple comparisons was used. For data with insufficient sample size to assess normality (Fig. 3h and Extended Data Fig. 5j–l), a Kruskal–Wallis test with Dunn’s multiple-comparison test was used. Simple linear regression was used to estimate relationship between serum testosterone and motility measurements. All analyses of mouse tissues, hormone levels and in vivo motility assays represent findings observed in at least two independent cohorts. Experiments were not randomized. Investigators were not blinded to allocation during experiments but were blinded to outcome assessment when feasible (imaging, neuronal

quantification, LC–MS/MS assays of hormone levels). All data was analyzed with GraphPad Prism version 10.0.2.

Data collection N/A

Data analysis Initial processing of metagenomic samples: Each metagenomic sample was processed through the workflow shown in Extended Data Fig.11. Raw metagenomic reads were trimmed, filtered, and assembled de novo into ORFs (open reading frames), using NGLess (v1.4.2) with default parameters 44. Generic feature format (GFF) files and predicted protein sequences were generated from the ORFs using Prodigal (v2.6.3) 45. Identification and characterization of GUS gene sequences: Metagenomic amino acid sequences were filtered for redundancies at a sequence identity threshold of 100% using CD-HIT (v4.8.1). These representative protein sequences were then used to identify putative GUS enzymes as reported previously 46,47. Accepted sequences were clustered again at 95% using CD-HIT, forming a representative set of GUS sequences for downstream analysis 48. Representative sequences were aligned to reference sequences from each loop class in a Multiple Sequence Alignment (MSA) using Clustal Omega, and GUS class was assigned according to parameters reported previously 46,47,49. Taxonomy was assigned to representative GUS sequences with a lowest common ancestor algorithm, using Diamond (v2.0.15.153) to map GUS representatives to proteins in the UHGP 47,50–52. Phylogenetic inference was performed on representative GUS sequences using Muscle5 (v5.1) 53 and IQ-TREE 2 (v2.2.0.3) 54. The resulting Newick tree file was combined with the GUS class and taxonomic annotations to create a cladogram (Extended Data Fig.7) using ggtree (v3.2.1) and ggplot2 in R (v4.1.2)55,56. Metagenomic gene intensity quantitation: For each sample, a bowtie2 index was created from the ORFs. A SAM file was then created by aligning the trimmed and filtered reads to the bowtie2 index. The SAM and GFF files were used to generate gene read counts in each sample, using featureCounts from the package SUBREAD (v2.0.1) (58). Gene read counts for all samples were then normalized based on the total reads detected in each sample and in all samples, yielding normalized intensity of each gene’s read count. These gene intensities were then filtered to only the representative GUS sequences. GUS gene intensities were further normalized to correct for the association between gene length and gene intensity. These methods were implemented exactly as reported in previous work (references 45,46).

## GREEN LABS: HOW SCIENTISTS CAN HELP FIGHT CLIMATE CHANGE

Julie Sesen, Stephanie Ragland, Valentina Lagomarsino and Sara Busatto *

The healthcare industry creates 4.4% of the world’s carbon emissions. To put this into perspective, if the healthcare industry were a country, it would be the ﬁfth-largest carbon emitter on the planet. The goal of the healthcare industry is to create new, life-saving treatments for patients, but it also produces a lot of waste that cannot be recycled, such as plastic and chemicals. Additionally, this industry uses a lot of non-renewable energy. The Green Lab Project is a worldwide, 10-year-old program attempting to reduce the carbon emissions caused by the activities of scientists within the healthcare industry. The Green Lab project arrived at Boston Children’s Hospital (BCH) in 2020, at the request of a group of postdocs, graduate students, and employees. The BCH Green Labs group is working to sponsor environment-protecting projects and educate BCH scientists to adopt more responsible, informed, and “greener” work practices. This article will describe ways that BCH scientists are trying to reduce lab waste and energy consumption, including sharing equipment and materials to limit waste production, cleaning freezers regularly, and using outlet timers to avoid wasting energy.

Researchers are becoming aware of the need to make research more environmentally friendly. All over the world, scientists are trying to ﬁnd innovative ways to be “greener”. Being greener means decreasing the environmental impact of their labs in terms of materials, water, energy, and waste production. Scientists can accomplish this goal with the help of numerous organizations. For instance, in the United States, we have two groups: My Green Lab and the International Institute for Sustainable Laboratories (I2SL). WHAT ARE BCH SCIENTISTS DOING TO BE GREENER?

Based on the discussions that BCH Green Labs had with the various hospital teams, here are some of the creative ways we have been trying to reduce BCH’s carbon footprint.

• The Freezer Challenge. Every year, BCH labs defrost and clean their big freezers, to reduce energy use and save time and money. At the same time, this initiative helps people develop good cold-storage practices that will hopefully become standard practice in the lab and be taught to future lab members. Did you know that most lab freezers are kept at −80◦C (four times colder than the freezer you have at home)? But they do not have to be! Increasing a freezer’s temperature by just a few degrees (from −80 to −70◦C) saves up to 30% of energy—this is about the amount of energy needed to power one home for a whole year! Crazy right? Importantly, a change of just 10◦C has little impact on the quality of the biological samples (urine, saliva, blood, etc.) being kept in the freezer, but this change can positively impact the environment!

Achievements so far: In 2022, BCH won the Top Clinical Organization Award of the International Freezer Challenge, organized by My Green Lab and I2SL, saving 463.8 kWh/day of energy, the equivalent of 16 households worth of energy saved daily.

• Share equipment, chemicals, and supplies. To reduce waste and save space, energy, and money, BCH labs decided to share instruments and materials instead of each lab buying their own. This simple practice helps reduce not only waste and energy consumption but also the number of shipments to BCH and the use of packaging material (e.g., non-recyclable plastic such as bubble wrap, ice packs, Styrofoam coolers, etc.).

Achievements so far: BCH Green Labs created a chemical inventory, to promote sharing of common chemicals among all BCH laboratories, signiﬁcantly reducing waste.

• Purchase sustainable lab products when possible: Over the years, an increasing number of sellers have begun to oﬀer products that are manufactured using less plastic and energy. Some companies have adjusted their shipping methods to minimize their impact, by replacing Styrofoam containers with cardboard boxes and using less plastic.

Achievements so far: Scientists often use plastic pipette tips to transfer minuscule amounts of liquids between containers. These tips are

Achievements so far: We have organized two outreach events, with an average of 40 attendants each. We have over 150 scientists subscribed to our newsletter.

## CONCLUSIONS

As the healthcare industry has a signiﬁcant impact on the global environment, it is essential for all scientists to work toward reducing healthcare’s carbon footprint. BCH is among the ﬁrst hospitals in the Boston area to implement a Green Lab initiative aimed at reducing, reusing, recycling, and responsibly disposing of medical waste. Green Lab initiatives worldwide could signiﬁcantly help in the ﬁght against climate change, by educating scientists and changing their behaviors in ways that would hopefully carry over to future generations.
